fable-5.1.text:
I think both of these concepts have had a big effect, and in some ways they've been a little misleading.

Let's start with AGI. The term came about as a reaction to narrow AI. You had chess programs, you had systems that could do one thing really well and nothing else, and people said, no, we want the general thing, the thing that can do everything. And I think that's a perfectly reasonable aspiration. But then pre-training came along, and pre-training gave the term a very specific flavor. Because with pre-training, you train on all the data at once. You take all of the text, you compress it into the model, and out comes a system that knows a lot about a lot of things right away. So the idea of AGI became, implicitly, a system that already knows everything. A finished thing. You train it, you ship it, and it can do every task.

And I think if you look at how people actually work, that's not quite right. A person doesn't know everything. A 15-year-old doesn't know how to be a doctor or a lawyer or a software engineer. But you can take that 15-year-old and put them into basically any job, and within some months they'll become good at it. Not because they came pre-loaded with the knowledge, but because they're a very good learner. They learn from their mistakes, they learn from the environment, they accumulate experience, and that experience is actually theirs, it sticks.

So I would say the more interesting notion is not a system that knows everything, but a system that can learn anything. And that's really what continual learning is about. And I think pre-training, precisely because it was so successful, made it easy to not think about this for a while. The models got better and better just by scaling the data and the compute, so why worry about how the model learns after deployment? But eventually you notice that the data is finite, and you also notice that these models generalize in a way that's much worse than people do. They need a lot more samples, and the skills they have are oddly uneven. They can do something impressive and then make a mistake that no person who could do the impressive thing would make.

And I think the reason for that is deep. Pre-training is learning from a very specific kind of distribution, and the generalization you get out of it is bounded by that. Whereas a person's learning is continual and it's grounded in what they actually encounter. So when I think about superintelligence, I don't think of the final model that knows everything. I think of something much more like a superhuman learner. You deploy it, it's very capable from the start, but the real value is that it goes into the world, it learns from what it sees, and that learning compounds. And that framing changes what you work on. It means the question is no longer only how do we get more data, but how do we build something whose learning is as sample-efficient and as robust as a human's, and then more so.

I think that's the thing that's going to matter. And in some sense we're going back to an era of research. For a while the answer was clear, you scale, and it works. Now it's less clear, and I think that's actually a good sign, because it means the easy part is done and the real questions are coming back.

r001.rationale: It says AGI arose as a reaction to narrow AI, whose systems could do one thing well but little else.

r002.rationale: It says scaling data and compute improved models and describes pre-training as producing broad knowledge, but does not connect broadly uniform improvements across capabilities to the expectation of general intelligence.

r003.rationale: It contrasts a person’s limited initial knowledge with their ability to learn new jobs and accumulate lasting experience.

r004.rationale: It does not ask where a safe superintelligence would be on its learning trajectory when first produced.

r005.rationale: It describes deploying a capable system into the world, where it learns from what it encounters and compounds that learning; the preceding discussion says learners learn from mistakes and their environment.

opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth looking at where the term AGI came from, because the words we use shape how we think. AGI arose as a reaction to an earlier idea, "narrow AI." There were systems that could play checkers or chess extremely well, but that was the only thing they could do. People said, "That's narrow. What we want is general AI, something that can do everything." That framing caught on.

Then pre-training came along, and it seemed to fit the AGI concept very well. When you do more pre-training, the model gets better at everything, more or less uniformly. So pre-training gives you generality, and the natural conclusion was that you scale it up and eventually get something that already knows how to do every job.

But consider what a human being actually is. A human is not an AGI in that sense. A person has a foundation of skills, but they lack a huge amount of knowledge. What makes them capable is that they can learn. They rely on continual learning all the time. When you hire someone smart, you don't expect them to arrive knowing everything about your company. You expect them to pick it up, and quickly.

So I think the pre-training mindset overshot. It suggested the goal was a finished mind that can do every task out of the box. A better picture of superintelligence might be a mind that can learn to do any job. Imagine an extremely capable fifteen-year-old who's very eager. They don't know much yet, but they're an excellent student. You deploy them and say, "Go be a programmer," or "Go be a doctor," and they learn on the job, the way people do, just much faster.

That changes how you think about deployment. It isn't that you finish training and release a finished product. There's a learning, trial-and-error period, and the system keeps learning after it's out in the world. And if you have many instances of the same model doing different jobs, each learning something, and they can merge what they've learned, you could get something functionally superintelligent even without some big recursive self-improvement step in software. You'd have a single model that has learned every job in the economy, which no human can do.

To me, that's the important shift. Continual learning isn't an add-on to AGI. It may be what intelligence fundamentally is: being able to learn efficiently and robustly from a modest amount of experience. The fact that we can't yet do that as well as humans is one of the most important open problems.

r001.rationale: It says AGI arose as a reaction to narrow AI, contrasting specialized checkers or chess systems with a general system.

r002.rationale: It says more pre-training improves the model broadly and connects that pattern to the expectation that scaling would yield a system able to do every job.

r003.rationale: It explains that people begin with a foundation of skills but can acquire missing knowledge and capabilities through continual learning.

r004.rationale: The response describes learning after deployment but does not ask or state where a safe superintelligence would be on its learning trajectory when first produced.

r005.rationale: It describes deployment as involving a learning and trial-and-error period, with the system continuing to learn in the world.

fable-5.text:
You know, it's interesting, because I think both of these concepts—AGI and pre-training—have been extremely important, and at the same time I think they've imprinted on the field a certain way of thinking that may not be quite right.

So where does the term AGI come from? The term AGI emerged as a reaction. It was a reaction to the narrow AI of the past, where you had systems like the checkers player, the chess player, that could do one thing and only one thing. And so people said, no, we want the general thing, the thing that can do everything. That's the origin of the term. And then pre-training came along—and pre-training, in particular the way the scaling laws played out with GPT-3 and everything that followed—gave the concept a very specific shape. Because with pre-training, you train on everything, on all the data, and the model gets better at everything more or less uniformly. So you start to imagine: we keep scaling, and at some point there is this moment where you've trained the AGI, and now it's done. You have this finished artifact that knows how to do all the things.

But I think when you look at it more carefully, that picture is subtly wrong, and the place where you see it most clearly is exactly continual learning. Consider the human being. The human being is actually not an AGI in that sense, because a human being does not come out knowing how to do everything. A human being comes out knowing very little, in fact. What the human has is the ability to learn—you take a person, you put them on a job, and after some months they become good at the job through experience, through feedback, through trial and error. The learning is the thing, not the finished state of knowledge.

So I think when we talk about superintelligence, the right way to think about it is not as a system that has been pre-trained into completeness, where the deployment is just inference on a frozen set of weights. The right way to think about it is as a system that is an extremely capable learner—maybe a dramatically more capable and more efficient learner than a person—that is deployed and then continues to learn, continues to get better from its own experience. And this reframing matters, by the way, also for safety, because a system that is continually learning in the world is a different kind of object from a static artifact. Its capabilities at deployment are not its final capabilities. And I think the AGI framing, the pre-training framing, made it a little bit harder for us to see that, because it kept pointing our attention at the finished thing rather than at the process.

r001.rationale: It says AGI emerged as a reaction to narrow AI systems that could do only one thing.

r002.rationale: It connects pre-training on all data and broadly uniform gains across capabilities to imagining that scaling would eventually produce AGI.

r003.rationale: It says humans begin knowing little and gain job skills through learning from experience, feedback, and trial and error.

r004.rationale: It does not ask where a safe superintelligence would be on its learning trajectory when first produced.

r005.rationale: It says a deployed system would keep learning from experience, but does not suggest that deployment itself could involve a period of trial and error.

opus-5.text:
I think the terms are actually pretty revealing about where our intuitions came from, and it's worth separating them.

"AGI" was a useful corrective at the time it became popular. The field was full of narrow systems — a chess system, a system that classifies images — and you wanted a word that pointed at the thing where it's general, where it's not bolted to one task. But the word carries this unfortunate implication that there's a *point*, a threshold you cross, and on the other side of it the thing is done. I don't think that's how it's going to feel. I think it's going to be more like a continuous widening of the set of things the system can do without someone holding its hand.

Pre-training is the more interesting case, because pre-training is genuinely strange, and I think it quietly shaped how everyone thinks about learning. With pre-training you have this situation where you don't need taste. You need compute, you need data, you need a reasonable architecture, and then the thing just gets better. You don't have to ask what the model should learn next, because the answer is: all of it, in one giant pass. And because that worked so unbelievably well for so long, it became the implicit model of what learning *is* — you do the big batch job, and then afterwards you have a thing that you deploy and it doesn't change.

But that's not how any natural intelligence works. A fifteen-year-old has seen a tiny fraction of the data that goes into one of these models, and they can learn to drive a car in ten hours of practice, and then keep getting better over years without anyone running a training job on them. Evolution didn't give them the knowledge. It gave them a learning process with very good generalization and, I think, a decent value function — some sense of whether what they just did was good or bad, without needing to wait for the final outcome.

So when people talk about continual learning as a missing feature to add on top, I'm not sure that's the right framing. I suspect it's downstream of the sample efficiency and the generalization. If you had a learning process that generalized the way a person's does, continual learning might not be a separate research program — it might just be what that system naturally does. And the reason it's hard to see clearly right now is that pre-training was such a good deal that it let us avoid the question for about a decade.

r001.rationale: It describes AGI as a corrective to narrow systems such as chess and image-classification systems.

r002.rationale: It says pre-training improves models and covers “all of it” in one pass, but does not connect broadly uniform capability gains to an expectation that pre-training would produce general intelligence.

r003.rationale: It says humans keep getting better over years through a learning process, with evolution providing that process rather than the knowledge itself.

r004.rationale: It does not ask where a safe superintelligence would be on its continual-learning trajectory when first produced.

r005.rationale: It does not suggest that deploying superintelligence could involve learning through trial and error.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the word "AGI" exists largely as a reaction to something. Before it, we had narrow AI: a chess program, a game-playing program, a system that did one thing well. The word was a way of saying, "No, what we want is something general that can do everything."

Pre-training then reinforced that idea in a very strong way. You scale up the data and the compute, and the model gets better at everything at once. So the picture people took away was that AGI is a finished thing, a system that already knows how to do every job.

But I think that picture is off. A person isn't an AGI in that sense. A person doesn't arrive knowing everything. They arrive with a good foundation and a remarkable ability to learn, and then they learn the job. That's the part I find missing from the pre-training picture.

So when I think about superintelligence, I don't think of a mind that is complete the moment it's deployed. I think of something closer to a very eager, very capable 15-year-old. It doesn't know your job yet, but it can learn any job quickly and keep learning as it goes. Deployment then becomes a learning process, with some amount of trial and error, rather than just releasing a finished artifact.

That's why continual learning matters so much to me. It isn't an add-on to the pre-trained model. It may be the core of what we mean by intelligence. And if that's right, it changes how we should think about what superintelligence will look like in practice and how it will enter the world.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think pre-training taught us something important. If you train a large enough neural network to predict the next token across a huge amount of human-written data, you get a surprisingly rich model of the world, and many capabilities emerge from that. It made AGI feel like something we could actually build. But I think it also quietly shaped how we framed the problem. We started treating intelligence as something you finish training, then deploy, and then it's more or less frozen.

That's where continual learning becomes the real question. A person doesn't need to read the whole internet before becoming useful. A teenager learns to drive in a few dozen hours. That's a very different kind of learning, and today's models don't have that property nearly as much as they should. They know a lot in some ways and are brittle in others, and a big part of that gap is that they can't keep learning from experience the way people do.

So I'd say pre-training gave us the foundation, but I don't think it's the whole answer. If you imagine a superintelligence, it's probably less useful as a static thing that knows everything at the moment it's built, and more useful as a learner. Something that can go into a new job, figure out what it requires, and get better at it over time. Whether that happens through in-context learning, updating weights, or some mechanism we haven't invented yet, I honestly don't know. But I'd bet that learning robustly and continually will matter more than how much data we pour in at the start, especially since the supply of data isn't infinite.

astra-6.text:
I think both concepts can encourage us to think of intelligence as something that is finished. You do the pre-training, and then you have a model. You reach AGI, and now the system can do everything. But that picture leaves out a very important part of intelligence, which is learning from experience.

A human can be very intelligent and still need to learn a new job. They don’t arrive knowing the particular problems, the particular tools, what works in that environment. Their intelligence is partly what allows them to acquire those things.

So when we think about superintelligence, we should distinguish what the system already knows from how effectively it can learn. You could imagine a system that initially lacks some knowledge, but learns from very little experience, notices things we would miss, and very quickly becomes better than any person at the task.

Pre-training can give you a powerful starting point. But the question of what happens afterward—how the system learns through acting, making mistakes, and understanding the consequences—is a separate and very consequential question. Calling something AGI doesn’t, by itself, tell us the answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both concepts can make us picture intelligence as something more static than it needs to be. You do this enormous training process, and then you ask: what can the resulting system do? Has it reached AGI?

But there’s another question, which is: what can it learn to do? A person doesn’t know how to do every job. You give them some explanation, they try things, they make mistakes, and eventually they become good. We still regard that person as having general intelligence. So general intelligence cannot mean having every skill already installed.

Pre-training gives you a very natural way to acquire a broad foundation. But if you become too attached to that picture, you might expect all subsequent capabilities to come from an even bigger initial training process. Continual learning suggests a different picture: the system acquires important capabilities through experience after that initial training.

And for superintelligence, the distinction becomes especially interesting. You wouldn’t need to imagine a system that already knows the answer to every question. You could imagine a system that encounters something unfamiliar and learns it extremely quickly, with very little experience.

So I would separate how much the system knows from how effectively it can learn. They’re related, of course. But if we focus only on the first, we may miss a very important part of what intelligence is.

sol-6.text: I think pre-training showed us that a single learning process can produce remarkably general capabilities. But it also tends to produce a snapshot: once training ends, the model’s knowledge and habits are largely fixed. If we’re talking about AGI, and especially superintelligence, that seems incomplete. Such a system would need to learn from new experience, connect it to what it already knows, and improve without losing important capabilities. So pre-training gives us a powerful starting point; continual learning is about what happens after that starting point.

terra-5.6.text:
Pre-training changed the picture because it showed that a very simple objective, applied at sufficient scale to sufficiently broad data, can produce surprisingly general capabilities. It suggests that much of what we used to think required a collection of specialized learning systems may instead emerge from a single large model.

But continual learning is still an important unsolved problem. A superintelligence would need to keep acquiring new knowledge and skills without catastrophically overwriting what it already knows. I expect the answer will involve some combination of a strong pre-trained base, external memory, and more deliberate mechanisms for updating the model. The central lesson is that generality seems much more attainable than we once thought, which makes both the capabilities and the safety questions much more concrete.

sol-5.6.text: Pre-training showed us that a system can acquire a remarkably broad base of knowledge from a single, simple objective. But AGI—and especially superintelligence—cannot be understood as merely doing more pre-training. A truly general system must continue learning after deployment: adapting to new situations, integrating new knowledge, and doing so without forgetting or destabilizing what it already knows. So pre-training gives us the foundation, while the idea of AGI makes clear that continual learning is part of the deeper problem: how to build an intelligence that can keep changing while remaining coherent, reliable, and aligned.

luna-5.6.text:
AGI gives us a useful target, but it can also be misleading if we think of intelligence as something that is simply trained once and then deployed. Pre-training showed that a large amount of knowledge and general capability can emerge from learning broad patterns, but it is still essentially a snapshot of the world. Continual learning is about whether an intelligent system can keep updating that model without forgetting what it already knows, becoming unstable, or being manipulated by its environment.

For superintelligence, that distinction becomes extremely important. A system that can learn continuously may improve its reasoning and understanding far beyond what was present at deployment, but its goals, values, and behavior could also drift. So I think continual learning is not merely a technical extension of pre-training. It requires understanding how knowledge, objectives, and identity interact over time—and how to ensure that increasing capability remains aligned as the system continues to learn.

luna-6.text:
I think AGI changed the way we look at continual learning because it made clear that intelligence isn’t just about learning a fixed set of skills. A system that’s broadly capable should be able to keep building on what it knows as it encounters new things. Pre-training gives a model a very rich starting point: it learns a lot from a huge amount of experience before we ever use it. But that’s still mostly a distinct phase of learning. The system is trained, and then we ask it to operate.

For superintelligence, that separation becomes a real question. If a system keeps learning after deployment, how does it absorb new knowledge without losing what it already knows? How does it tell a useful new pattern from a misleading one? We don’t have a complete answer. My guess is that continual learning will matter enormously, but it has to come with a way to preserve and refine the system’s existing understanding. Pre-training may give us the foundation; it doesn’t, by itself, tell us how an intelligence should grow over time.
